options: A transaction's changes either all happen or none do
questions.explanation: Atomicity means no partial transactions: if any step fails, everything rolls back.

questions.prompt: Which constraint ensures no two customers share the same email?
questions.explanation: UNIQUE rejects duplicates. NOT NULL only forbids missing values; CHECK tests a condition per row; FOREIGN KEY references another table.

questions.prompt: A database test should run against a disposable or dedicated test database, never against shared production data.
questions.explanation: Tests create, change and delete data. Isolated databases keep them repeatable and safe.

questions.prompt: Two users try to buy the last ticket at the same time and both succeed. Which kind of test would have caught this?
options: A concurrency test that runs both transactions in parallel and checks the stock never goes below zero
A unit test of the price calculation
questions.explanation: Race conditions only show up when operations overlap. Constraints (CHECK stock >= 0), locking or atomic updates prevent them, and concurrent tests prove it.

questions.prompt: Which should a database migration test check? Select all that apply.
options: The migration runs on a copy of realistic, production-sized data within the maintenance window
Existing data is preserved and transformed correctly
The migration file name is alphabetical
questions.explanation: Migrations fail on real data volume, edge-case values and rollback. File naming conventions matter for ordering, but are not what a test validates.

questions.prompt: What does this return when `discount` is NULL for one of three rows (values 10, NULL, 20)?
questions.explanation: AVG ignores NULLs, so it averages 10 and 20 = 15. COUNT(discount) would be 2, while COUNT(*) is 3.

questions.prompt: This transfer sometimes leaves money missing after a crash between the two statements. What is the fix?
options: Wrap both updates in one transaction (BEGIN ... COMMIT) so a failure rolls both back
Swap the order of the updates
Run the updates in two separate connections
questions.explanation: Without a transaction, each statement commits separately (autocommit), so a crash between them loses the money. A single transaction makes the transfer atomic.

questions.prompt: A stored procedure produces correct totals in tests with 100 rows but times out in production with 20 million. What testing gap does this show, and how do you close it?
options: No volume testing: run database tests against production-like data volumes and check execution plans
Missing unit tests for the UI
Production has a different SQL language
questions.explanation: Functional correctness at small scale says nothing about performance at large scale. Representative volume and EXPLAIN plans close the gap.

coding.title: Find duplicate emails
coding.prompt:
Data-quality check: list every email that appears more than once in `customers` (compare case-insensitively, output in lower case) with its count as `n`, ordered by email.

Expected: `ana@x.test | 2`, `ravi@x.test | 3`.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT 1 AS placeholder;
coding.solution: SELECT LOWER(email) AS email, COUNT(*) AS n FROM customers GROUP BY LOWER(email) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY email;
coding.explanation: Normalising with LOWER before grouping finds duplicates that a case-sensitive UNIQUE constraint would allow. HAVING filters on the aggregated count.
coding.setup:
CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT);
INSERT INTO customers (email) VALUES ('ana@x.test'),('ANA@x.test'),('bo@x.test'),('ravi@x.test'),('Ravi@x.test'),('ravi@X.test');

coding.title: Reconcile balances with the ledger
coding.prompt:
Each account's `balance` should equal the sum of its `ledger.amount` rows. List `account_id`, `balance` and `ledger_total` for accounts where they differ (treat no ledger rows as 0), ordered by `account_id`.

Expected: `2 | 50 | 40`, `3 | 10 | 0`.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT 1 AS placeholder;
coding.solution: SELECT a.account_id, a.balance, COALESCE(SUM(l.amount), 0) AS ledger_total FROM accounts a LEFT JOIN ledger l ON l.account_id = a.account_id GROUP BY a.account_id, a.balance HAVING a.balance <> COALESCE(SUM(l.amount), 0) ORDER BY a.account_id;
coding.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps accounts with no ledger rows; COALESCE turns their NULL sum into 0 so the comparison works. Reconciliation queries like this catch lost or double-applied transactions.
hints: SUM is NULL with no rows: wrap it in COALESCE.
